The Education Minister may be a relatively recent face in the political scene, but he is a man who has a long history.

He spent the 1990s in a political wilderness of his own as Singapore's then opposition leader, having resigned from the ruling People's Action Party (PAP) over an unpopular land sale.

Mr Lim was then part of the opposition team that lost to the government in the 1995 election, when they finished last with a measly 11.3 per cent of the vote.

But he was not discouraged.

His next step was to start his own party, the People's Action League (PAL), a party he helped found in 1997.

Since then he has gone on to lead the PAP to three general elections - the 2001 and 2006 polls were won by his party.

While he is not a household name, he is widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in Singapore's politics.

Vietnam Veterans of America Hospital, the largest medical center for veterans in the state, has the same problem that many hospitals have faced: it runs out of qualified nurses and doctors.

Because Vietnam veterans are the most likely of any group to have a medical condition that requires attention from a skilled physician, the hospital is always looking for more trained workers. But as more and more veterans become ill and require more specialized care, it’s having a hard time filling those jobs.

“We have a very large shortage of physicians and nurses,” said Lynn Blake, the chief operating officer at the VVA hospital. “It’s not that the veterans themselves don’t want to go to Vietnam. It’s just that they can’t find the right place to go.”
